learn.hook: Sailors on the Indian Ocean trade routes trusted the magnetic compass centuries ago. The same lodestone magic now spins hard disks and runs EV motors.
points: Magnetism is found naturally (lodestone). The Earth itself behaves like a huge magnet whose field points roughly from the geographic south to the geographic north, so a freely suspended magnet settles roughly along the north-south line.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Cutting a magnet only gives smaller magnets: isolated poles do not exist.
Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet trace a pattern just like that of a current-carrying solenoid.
Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops (outside from N to S, inside from S to N), never intersect, the tangent gives B, and their crowding shows the field's strength.
Unlike electric field lines, which start and end on charges, magnetic field lines have no start or end.

example.q: A bar magnet is cut into two equal pieces across its length. What do you get?
steps: Each piece develops a new N and S at the cut.
Each piece is a complete, weaker magnet.
example.answer: Two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S pole

learn.reallife: MRI scanners at AIIMS, Delhi, use superconducting coils whose field lines loop through the patient, just like the closed loops around a bar magnet.

Each piece is a new dipole.
The iron filing pattern of a bar magnet resembles that of a solenoid.

quiz.q: Which statement about magnetic field lines is correct?
options: They begin at the north pole and end at the south pole inside the magnet
They can intersect where the field is strong
quiz.explain: Outside N to S, inside S to N: always closed.
quiz.mistake: Treats magnetic lines like electrostatic ones

quiz.q: A bar magnet is cut into three equal pieces by two cuts perpendicular to its axis. How many magnetic poles are there in total?
quiz.explain: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with N and S, so 3 × 2 = 6 poles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cut pieces lose their poles

quiz.q: Inside a bar magnet, the direction of the magnetic field lines is
options: from the north pole to the south pole
from the south pole to the north pole
zero, there are no lines inside
quiz.explain: Field lines must be closed, so inside they return from S to N.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lines end at the south pole

quiz.q: What does the crowding of magnetic field lines in a region indicate?
quiz.explain: Line density represents field strength.

quiz.q: A freely suspended bar magnet comes to rest roughly along the north-south line because
options: the Earth behaves like a giant magnet
the magnet is attracted by the North Star
quiz.explain: The Earth's magnetic field exerts a torque that aligns the magnet.

quiz.q: Iron filings around a current-carrying solenoid show a pattern similar to that of
quiz.explain: A solenoid's field is a dipole field like a bar magnet's.
quiz.mistake: Compares with a straight wire's circular field

quiz.q: Why can two magnetic field lines never cross?
options: At the crossing point, B would have two directions
quiz.explain: A field has one direction at a point; the tangent to a single line gives it.
quiz.mistake: Gives the closed-loop property as the reason

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops. Reason (R): Isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Without monopoles, there is nowhere for magnetic lines to start or end, so they must close on themselves.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the absence of monopoles with closed field lines

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where do the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet end?'
teach.praise: Chirp! They never end: they run N to S outside and S to N inside, forming closed loops. Endless!
teach.nudge: Good! Do the lines stop at the south pole, or continue inside the magnet?

topics.title: The bar magnet as a magnetic dipole

learn.hook: Cut a solenoid open in your imagination and you will find a bar magnet inside. Their fields are so alike that we use the same formulas for both.
points: A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid: its magnetism comes from tiny circulating currents in its atoms. Its magnetic moment m points along its axis from S to N.
Far field on the axis: B = (µ₀/4π)(2m/r³), along m.
Far field on the equatorial line: B = -(µ₀/4π)(m/r³), opposite to m.
The magnetic moment can be found from the field it produces, or from the torque it feels in a known field (τ = mB sinθ).
A neutral point is where the magnet's field exactly cancels another field (such as Earth's horizontal field); a compass there shows no preferred direction.

example.q: A short bar magnet has m = 0.5 A m². Find B on its axis at 10 cm.

learn.reallife: Fridge-door magnets and the magnetic catches on almirahs in Indian homes are small dipoles; their field falls off as 1/r³, which is why they grip only at very short range.

quiz.explain: Like the electric dipole (from -q to +q), m points from S to N.

quiz.explain: Axial 2m vs equatorial m in the formulas.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How is a bar magnet like a solenoid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A bar magnet is like a solenoid made of tiny atomic current loops, with the same dipole field pattern. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good! Compare their field patterns. What is the source of magnetism inside a magnet?

topics.title: A magnetic dipole in a uniform field

learn.hook: Flick a compass needle and it oscillates before settling. Count those oscillations and you can actually compare magnetic fields, an old trick of field scientists.
points: A magnetic dipole in uniform B feels no net force but a torque τ = m × B, magnitude mB sinθ, turning m towards B.
Its potential energy is U = -m·B = -mB cosθ: minimum (stable) at θ = 0, maximum (unstable) at θ = 180°.
A compass needle disturbed from equilibrium oscillates; a stronger field gives a stronger restoring torque and faster oscillations, so oscillation rates can compare fields.
Electrostatic analogue: replace p by m and 1/(4πε₀) by µ₀/4π. Then E-dipole formulas give B-dipole formulas.
Analogy table: torque p × E ↔ m × B; energy -p·E ↔ -m·B; axial field 2p/(4πε₀r³) ↔ µ₀2m/(4πr³).

example.q: A magnet of m = 2 A m² is at 60° to a 0.1 T field. Find the torque and the energy.

learn.reallife: Before electronic magnetometers, surveyors compared the strength of magnetic fields at different places by timing the oscillations of a freely suspended magnet: the faster it oscillated, the stronger the field.

quiz.explain: τ = mB sin90° = 0.3 N m.

quiz.explain: U = -mB cos0° = -1 J.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a compass needle swing back and forth before stopping?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The torque mB sinθ keeps pulling it back to the low-energy position, so it oscillates before settling. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! What torque acts on the needle, and where is its energy lowest?

learn.hook: Draw any closed bubble around a magnet, around half a magnet, or around nothing at all. The magnetic flux through it is always exactly zero.
points: Gauss's law for magnetism: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: ∮B·dS = 0.
Every field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, because magnetic field lines are closed loops.
This expresses the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist; the simplest magnetic source is a dipole.
Contrast: in electrostatics, ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, which can be non-zero because electric charges exist.
Flux through an open surface (not closed) can be non-zero; the law is only about closed surfaces.

example.q: A closed surface surrounds only the north pole end of a bar magnet. What is the net magnetic flux through it?
steps: Field lines leave near the north pole...
...but lines inside the magnet enter the surface from the south side.
Every line that leaves also enters, so the net flux is zero.

learn.reallife: Physicists at India's research labs, like many worldwide, have searched for magnetic monopoles in cosmic rays. None have been found, consistent with Gauss's law for magnetism.

quiz.explain: Gauss's law for magnetism: ∮B·dS = 0 for any closed surface.

quiz.explain: Net flux zero means lines in = lines out.

options: Electric charges exist, but magnetic monopoles do not
Magnetic fields only exist inside magnets
quiz.explain: Electric lines start and end on charges; magnetic lines have no ends.

quiz.explain: Lines entering from outside near the S pole leave through the part of the magnet inside the surface; the total is zero.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the south pole acts as a sink

quiz.explain: For an open surface flux = BA = 0.1 Wb; Gauss's law (zero) applies only to closed surfaces.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed loops cross any closed surface an even number of times, in and out.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect closed loops with zero flux

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I wrap a bubble around the north pole of a magnet, will magnetic flux pour out?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Every line that leaves also enters, because there are no monopoles. Net flux zero!
teach.nudge: Close! Follow the lines inside the magnet. Do they also cross your bubble?

learn.hook: Slide an iron rod into a solenoid and the field inside can jump hundreds of times. The material itself joins in. Here is how we describe that.
points: Magnetisation M = net magnetic moment per unit volume (unit A m⁻¹).
Magnetic intensity H is defined by B = µ₀(H + M). In a solenoid, H = nI (from the free current), unit A m⁻¹.
For many materials M = χH, where χ (dimensionless) is the magnetic susceptibility. Then B = µ₀(1 + χ)H = µ₀µrH = µH.
Relative permeability µr = 1 + χ; permeability µ = µ₀µr.
χ is small and negative for diamagnets (bismuth about -1.66 × 10⁻⁵), small and positive for paramagnets (aluminium about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵), and very large and positive for ferromagnets.

example.q: A solenoid with n = 800 m⁻¹ carries 2.5 A and has a core of µr = 500. Find H, B and M. (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷, π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Transformer cores at Indian substations use special silicon steel with a very large relative permeability, so a modest current produces a large magnetic flux.

quiz.q: A material has χ = 499. What is its relative permeability?
A solenoid has n = 500 turns per metre and carries 4 A. What is H inside (in A m⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: H = nI = 500 × 4 = 2000 A m⁻¹. (This does not depend on the core.)
quiz.mistake: Thinks H depends on the core

quiz.q: A material in a field H = 1000 A m⁻¹ has χ = 2 × 10⁻⁵. What is its magnetisation (in A m⁻¹)?
A core with µr = 1000 is in a solenoid where H = 500 A m⁻¹. What is B inside (in T)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, π = 3.14)
The relation between B, H and M is
quiz.explain: Both the free current (through H) and the material (through M) contribute to B.

quiz.q: Which material has a negative magnetic susceptibility?
quiz.explain: Bismuth is diamagnetic, with χ about -1.66 × 10⁻⁵.

quiz.q: Magnetisation M is defined as
options: net magnetic moment per unit volume
magnetic moment per unit mass only
quiz.explain: M = m_net/V, measured in A m⁻¹.

quiz.q: A material with µr = 0.99999 placed in a field is
quiz.explain: µr < 1 means χ < 0: diamagnetic. A superconductor would have µr = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks µr just below 1 means paramagnetic

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do H, M and B each mean inside an iron-cored coil?'
teach.praise: Chirp! H comes from the coil's current, M from the material's moments, and B = µ₀(H + M). Iron core power!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each of H and M represent, and how do they combine to give B?

learn.hook: A live frog was once levitated in a strong magnet because water in its body is diamagnetic. Even 'non-magnetic' things respond to magnetic fields.
points: Classification by χ: diamagnetic (χ small, negative), paramagnetic (χ small, positive), ferromagnetic (χ large, positive).
Diamagnets are weakly repelled; they move from stronger to weaker field regions, and field lines are slightly pushed out of them. Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, nitrogen at STP.
Superconductors cooled below their critical temperature expel the field completely (χ = -1, µr = 0): the Meissner effect. They are perfect diamagnets.
Paramagnets have atoms with permanent magnetic moments. A field partly aligns them against thermal randomness, so they are weakly attracted, moving from weak to strong field regions.
Examples of paramagnets: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen at STP, copper chloride.

example.q: A bar of bismuth and a bar of aluminium are hung freely between the poles of a strong magnet. How do they settle?
steps: Bismuth is diamagnetic, so it moves away from the strongest field.
It settles perpendicular to the field.
Aluminium is paramagnetic and settles along the field.
example.answer: Bismuth across the field; aluminium along the field

learn.reallife: Japan's experimental SCMaglev train floats on powerful superconducting magnets, and in science exhibitions a small superconductor cooled with liquid nitrogen can be seen hovering above a magnet because it pushes the field out (perfect diamagnetism).

moves from the weaker to the stronger region
quiz.explain: Diamagnets are repelled, so they move towards weaker fields.

quiz.q: Which gas at STP is paramagnetic?
quiz.explain: Oxygen molecules have a net magnetic moment and are weakly attracted.

Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is it true that a magnet can push away water?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Yes, water is diamagnetic: it is weakly repelled and moves towards weaker field. Frog-floating physics!
teach.nudge: Good! What kind of magnetic material is water, and how does it respond to a field?

learn.hook: Why is iron so dramatically magnetic while aluminium barely notices a magnet? The answer lies in tiny regions called domains.
points: In ferromagnets (iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium), atomic moments line up spontaneously in small regions called domains, each about 1 mm across.
Normally domains point randomly. An applied field grows the domains aligned with it and rotates others, giving a huge M and very large χ; they are strongly attracted.
Hard ferromagnets (alnico, used for permanent magnets) keep their magnetisation; soft ferromagnets (soft iron, used in electromagnets and transformer cores) lose it when the field is removed.
Above a certain temperature, the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic.
Problem tips: sign of χ classifies the material; in a non-uniform field, ferromagnets and paramagnets move to stronger fields, diamagnets to weaker fields.

example.q: An iron nail is attracted to a magnet but loses that property after strong heating. Explain.
steps: Iron is ferromagnetic because of aligned domains.
Heating above the Curie temperature destroys the spontaneous alignment.
The nail becomes paramagnetic, only weakly attracted.
example.answer: Heating above the Curie temperature makes iron lose its ferromagnetism

learn.reallife: Permanent magnets in the motors of Indian-made electric two-wheelers are hard ferromagnets, while the cores of electromagnets in scrapyard cranes in Alang are soft iron.

games.title: Domain facts

quiz.q: Which of these is ferromagnetic at room temperature?
quiz.explain: Iron, cobalt and nickel are the common ferromagnets.

quiz.q: What explains the strong magnetism of ferromagnetic materials?
options: Domains in which atomic moments are spontaneously aligned
quiz.explain: Aligned domains add up to a very large magnetisation.

quiz.q: Why is soft iron used for the core of an electromagnet?
options: It magnetises strongly in a field and loses its magnetisation when the current is switched off
quiz.explain: A soft ferromagnet responds strongly but does not retain magnetisation.

quiz.q: A ferromagnet heated above its Curie temperature becomes
quiz.explain: Domain alignment is destroyed but atoms keep their moments.

quiz.explain: χ can be in the thousands for ferromagnets.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ferromagnetic and paramagnetic values

quiz.q: A material with χ = -2 × 10⁻⁵ is placed near the pole of a strong magnet. It will
quiz.explain: Negative χ means diamagnetic: weakly repelled.

quiz.q: Which material would be the best choice for a permanent magnet?
quiz.explain: Hard ferromagnets retain their magnetisation.
quiz.mistake: Picks soft iron because it magnetises easily

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An unmagnetised iron bar shows no net magnetism. Reason (R): Its domains are oriented randomly, so their moments cancel. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Randomly oriented domains give zero net moment until a field aligns them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks unmagnetised iron has no domains

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is iron so much more magnetic than aluminium?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Iron is ferromagnetic: its domains of aligned atomic moments line up in a field. Aluminium is only weakly paramagnetic!
teach.nudge: Good! What are domains, and what happens to them in a field?
